title: The Phenomenology of the Munich and Göttingen Circles

summaries.example: Imagine hearing a friend say, “Please pass the ball.” You see and hear the words, but you also understand what your friend wants you to do. The phenomenologists would say that seeing the words and understanding their meaning are different kinds of mental acts.
summaries.summary: The Munich and Göttingen circles were early twentieth-century groups of phenomenologists. Phenomenology tries to describe experiences carefully rather than reducing every question to psychology. These philosophers studied how minds are directed toward things, a feature called intentionality. They distinguished presentations, such as seeing or imagining, from meaning acts, such as understanding a word or thinking about an object. They also examined attitudes: beliefs, emotions, wishes, and decisions. Their work explored how people understand one another, how promises and orders work, and how groups can share experiences. In ontology, the study of what exists, many members defended the view that objects, facts, and values have natures that do not depend simply on someone's beliefs. They disagreed about some important questions, including whether reality is independent of consciousness and which states of affairs truly exist.
key_ideas: The Munich and Göttingen circles were groups of philosophers who studied experience, thinking, values, actions, and the world.
They argued that seeing something and thinking about what it means may be different mental acts.
People can take different attitudes toward what they notice: they can believe it, care about it, or decide to act.
They studied how people understand one another through speech, empathy, and shared group experiences.
Many of them thought that objects and facts have their own nature and do not depend only on someone's thoughts.
summaries.why_it_matters: This tradition helps us notice that thinking is richer than simply having pictures in our heads. Seeing, understanding words, believing, caring, and deciding can all relate to the same thing in different ways. Its ideas also help us ask careful questions about friendship, communication, teamwork, values, and the difference between what people think and what is actually the case.

important_terms.definition: A way of studying experience by carefully describing what appears in our minds and in the world around us.
The way some thoughts, feelings, and other mental acts are directed toward something, such as a tree, a question, or a person.
An experience in which something is given to us through perception or imagination, such as seeing a ball or picturing one.
A mental act of thinking about or referring to something, even when the thing is not right in front of us.
A position or stance we take, such as believing something, feeling about it, or deciding to do something.
The idea that some things, including objects and facts, exist whether or not anyone is thinking about them.

questions_to_think_about: Is seeing a red apple the same as thinking, “That is an apple”?
Can you understand that someone is sad without feeling sad yourself?
What is the difference between wanting to help and deciding how to help?
When does a group truly share an experience?

summaries.example: Suppose a student sees two lines in an optical illusion. The lines look unequal, yet the student believes they are equal after learning how the illusion works. Early phenomenologists use cases like this to distinguish presentation from belief: perception gives an appearance, while belief is a doxastic attitude that can oppose or agree with what appears. The two acts may concern the same object without being the same experience.
summaries.summary: The Munich and Göttingen circles developed an early form of realist phenomenology influenced especially by Edmund Husserl, while also criticizing parts of his account. Their central contribution to philosophy of mind is a pluralistic theory of intentionality. Rather than treating all mental directedness as one basic relation, many members distinguished meaning acts, presentations, and attitudes. Presentations provide intuitive access through perception or imagination; meaning acts refer linguistically without making an object intuitively present. On the basis of cognition, subjects can adopt doxastic, affective, or conative attitudes: they can believe, respond emotionally, or will an end. Willing was treated as distinct from mere desire because it involves a disposition toward decision and action. The circles also analyzed social acts, empathy, and collective experiences. A promise or order requires uptake by an addressee, empathy involves access to another person's experience without simply living that experience oneself, and groups differ according to whether members are mentally infected, rationally coordinated, or sharing an experience as ours. Their ontology distinguished objects from states of affairs and connected necessity to essences, while debates continued over which states of affairs exist independently of intentionality.
key_ideas: The circles opposed psychologism, the attempt to explain logic, ethics, or metaphysics entirely in psychological terms.
Many members defended realist phenomenology: objects and facts have structures and essential properties that are not created by a person's beliefs.
Meaning acts and presentations can share a reference while differing in kind; the former are linguistic and non-intuitive, while the latter provide intuitive access.
Cognitions can ground attitudes: a person may first encounter a fact, then believe it, feel about it, or will an action in response.
Empathy was often explained as perceiving another's mental state in expressive behavior, not necessarily as reproducing that state inside oneself.
The circles distinguished crowds, societies, and communities according to whether experiences spread without reasons, are coordinated through reasons, or are genuinely shared as ours.
summaries.why_it_matters: The tradition offers a detailed vocabulary for separating experiences that ordinary speech often blends together. It clarifies why perceiving, believing, feeling a value, wanting, and intending are not interchangeable. Its analyses of promises, empathy, and collective life also connect philosophy of mind with language, ethics, social theory, and the study of institutions. Finally, its realism-idealism dispute raises a lasting question: how can consciousness be involved in our access to reality without making reality depend entirely on consciousness?

important_terms.definition: A philosophical method and tradition that describes the essential structures of experience, objects, values, and social relations.
Directedness toward an object, fact, or state of affairs. Early Munich and Göttingen thinkers often treated different forms of directedness as fundamentally distinct.
An intuitive experience, such as perception or imagination, through which an object is given or made present to consciousness.
An essentially linguistic and non-intuitive act of referring to or thinking about something; it is not simply a weaker presentation.
An active stance toward an object or fact, including doxastic attitudes such as belief, affective attitudes such as emotion, and conative attitudes such as willing.
A way of grasping a value-property, such as beauty or danger, receptively rather than by merely adopting an emotion toward it.
The study of what exists and how different kinds of entities, including objects and states of affairs, are structured.
An entity that makes a proposition true or false, according to one influential view in the circles; philosophers disagreed about which such entities exist independently of minds.

questions_to_think_about: If perception and belief can conflict, which experience should guide judgment, and why?
Can a mental state be directly perceived in a person's expression, or must it be inferred?
Does a promise differ from a report about what someone wants because it creates a special claim or obligation?
What conditions make an experience genuinely collective rather than merely similar across individuals?
Does the existence of a social object, such as an obligation, challenge a simple division between mental and physical things?

summaries.example: Imagine that your class sees a surprising science demonstration. Everyone notices the same event, but students respond differently. One believes the explanation, another feels excited, and a third decides to investigate further. The phenomenologists would separate the shared presentation of the event from these different attitudes. They might also ask whether the class has a collective experience: are students merely copying one another's excitement, cooperating for a reason, or experiencing the event together as “our” discovery?
summaries.summary: The Munich and Göttingen circles were networks of early twentieth-century philosophers who used phenomenology to investigate mind, language, values, social life, and reality. They opposed psychologism, the view that logical or ethical principles can be explained only as facts about human psychology. Many members instead supported a realist outlook: objects and facts have their own structures, even though minds can know them. In their philosophy of mind, they emphasized that intentionality may have several basic forms. A presentation gives intuitive access through perception or imagination, while a meaning act refers through language and does not itself display the object. After encountering something, a person may adopt an attitude toward it: a doxastic attitude such as belief, an affective attitude such as concern, or a conative attitude such as willing. The philosophers also investigated speech acts, empathy, and collective experiences. Promises and orders need to be understood by their addressees; empathy can involve perceiving another person's experience in their expression; and groups may be crowds, societies, or communities depending on how members' experiences are connected. In ontology, they discussed objects, essences, and states of affairs, but they did not all agree about which facts exist independently of minds.
key_ideas: The philosophers rejected psychologism, which treated logic and other philosophical areas as parts of psychology.
They often believed reality contains objects and facts that are not made by our opinions.
They distinguished direct or intuitive experience from thinking through words.
Believing, feeling, and willing are different ways of taking a position toward something.
They studied communication acts, empathy, and the different ways people form groups.
They disagreed about whether reality is independent of consciousness and about which facts exist on their own.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas can sharpen how we think about everyday experiences. A person can notice an event without believing a particular explanation, recognize a value without feeling an emotion, and want a goal without deciding how to reach it. The circles also show why communication and teamwork are philosophical topics: a promise, a shared plan, and a crowd's excitement involve different structures. Their disagreements give students practice in comparing theories rather than assuming that one simple description fits every mental or social experience.

important_terms.definition: A philosophy that carefully examines how things are experienced and understood, including objects, feelings, actions, and relationships.
The mind's directedness toward something, such as an object, fact, goal, or another person's experience.
A perception or imagination that gives an object some intuitive presence, such as seeing a demonstration or picturing it.
An act of thinking or referring to something through language, without needing that thing to be visibly present.
A stance toward something. The main types discussed are belief-like, emotional, and goal-directed attitudes.
Understanding another person's experience through expressive movements or gestures, without literally having the same experience.
The study of what exists, including the kinds of objects, facts, values, and social entities there are.
A fact-like structure, such as a rose's being red, toward which a judgment or belief can be directed.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people see the same event but have different attitudes toward it?
Is understanding someone's sadness the same as feeling sad too?
Why might an order or promise be more than a description of what a person wants?
What separates a crowd from a community?
Are facts created by minds, or can they exist independently of what anyone thinks?
